name: The Database Verifier
oneLiner: One reconciliation engine that checks a displayed value against the record behind it — seven compare modes, pure and offline, no DB required.
lead: A single `compare()` engine that reconciles a source-of-truth value against a value-under-test across seven modes — exact, numeric tolerance, set, contains, presence, empty, count. It's a pure function with no I/O, so the comparison logic needs no database, network, or credentials. Optional `jsonPath()` extraction and a direct-or-bridge SQL backend feed it real data when you go live; the same `compare()` runs in both.
chore: The prior setup meant opening the source records by hand, reading the real value, then flipping to the app to eyeball a match. Slow, mind-numbing, and easy to miss a subtle mismatch — a trailing space, a differently-formatted date, a same-set list in a different order.
instead: One `compare()` engine takes two values, a mode, and returns a typed pass/fail with a reason. It normalizes both sides first — `trim`, `lower`, `date` — so a cosmetic difference isn't a false fail. It runs as a pure function, no DB attached; when you need real records, a direct connection or a folder-relay bridge fetches them, but the comparison itself is I/O-free and trivially unit-testable.
whyItMatters: Catching a silent mismatch between what users see and what is actually stored prevents the kind of quiet data error that erodes trust in a whole system — and because `compare()` is a pure function, that logic is unit-testable with zero infrastructure.

howItWorks.step: `normalizeVal` applies a comma-list of ops — `trim`, `lower`, `date` — to both sides before comparison, so a cosmetic difference doesn't fail a real match.
howItWorks.explain: The false-positive filter: before any comparison, both expected and actual are pushed through the **same** comma-separated op chain, so a purely cosmetic difference never grades as a real mismatch. Ops apply in written order and each is type-guarded — `trim`/`lower` only touch strings, while `date` parses via `new Date()` and reformats to `YYYY-MM-DD` (`toISOString().slice(0, 10)`) but on an unparseable value (`isNaN(getTime())`) **leaves the original untouched** rather than emitting `Invalid Date`. Arrays are mapped element-wise through the inner `one()`, so a list normalizes per item. No ops string means the value returns unchanged — normalization is strictly opt-in.

howItWorks.step: `compare` reads one `ReconCheck` (name, mode, expected, actual), normalizes both sides, and routes to whichever of the seven modes the check asked for — returning a `ReconResult` with a plain reason.
howItWorks.explain: The reconciliation engine — a **pure function with zero I/O**, which is what makes it unit-testable with no database. It lowercases the mode and **defaults to `exact`** if unrecognized, normalizes both sides through `normalizeVal` with the check's `normalize` ops, then `switch`es to one of the seven mode branches. Two are shown: `set` uses `setEq` for **order-insensitive** membership (so `[a,b]` equals `[b,a]`), while `exact`/default compares canonical `JSON.stringify(tryJson(...))` on both sides so structurally-equal values match regardless of key spacing. Every branch funnels through the `done()` closure to return a `ReconResult` carrying `pass` plus a human-readable `detail` — the reason is always spelled out, never a bare boolean.

howItWorks.step: `jsonPath` pulls the actual value out of an API JSON body — dotted paths, array indexes, a `[*]` wildcard that fans out over a list, and a trailing `.length` for counts.
howItWorks.explain: Extracts the value-under-test out of an API JSON body with a compact path grammar. It first rewrites bracket syntax `[0]`/`[*]` into dotted segments (`.0`/`.*`) so a single split on `.` handles both. The clever bit is the **frontier**: `cur` is always an array of live nodes, and a `*` segment **fans out** by pushing every element of each array node — so `data.regions[*].name` walks from `[body]` to the regions array to a list of names. Missing nodes are skipped (`node == null` continue), so a bad path yields empty rather than throwing. When the expression contained `[*]` it returns the whole `cur` list (feeding a set or count check); otherwise it unwraps to the single element, and a trailing `.length` on a fanned-out list is how a count-mode check gets its number.

howItWorks.step: `BridgeBackend.query` runs SQL two ways — a direct connection, or a file-drop 'bridge' for databases only reachable from a locked-down host.
howItWorks.explain: The **inbox/outbox file bridge** for a database only reachable from a locked-down host that has no driver or network path installed here. It writes the SQL to a uniquely-named `{id}.sql` in a shared `inbox/` — the id combines `Date.now()` with a random suffix to avoid collisions between concurrent queries — then **polls** `outbox/` every 2 s for a `{id}.done` marker until `timeoutSec` (default 300) elapses. The `.done` file is the completion signal: a helper on the secured host runs the SQL and writes both the marker and a `{id}.csv`, and only once the marker exists does this read and `parseCsv` the result. On timeout it throws `[db] bridge timeout waiting for {name}`, so a stalled bridge fails loudly instead of hanging forever.

howItWorks.step: `reconStep` converts a `ReconResult` into the same `EvidenceStep` shape the API tester emits, so DB and API checks render side by side in one report.
howItWorks.explain: The adapter that lets DB checks share a report with API checks: it converts a `ReconResult` into the very same `EvidenceStep` shape the API tester emits, differing only by `kind: 'db'`, so the shared report builder colour-codes and lays them out identically. The `pass` boolean maps to a `'pass'`/`'fail'` `Verdict` (what drives green vs red), the mode and expected value go into `req`, and the actual value plus the `detail` reason go into `resp`; both values are `display()`d with a 120-char cap so a large field can't blow out the panel. Because API and DB evidence are structurally identical, a single dashboard can show them **side by side**.

examples.caption: Confirm a displayed total matches the record
examples.output: A green pass reading 'equal', logged as an `EvidenceStep` — no DB or network for the comparison itself.

examples.caption: Ignore a cosmetic formatting difference
examples.input: Record date `2026-07-21` vs app value `' 2026-07-21 '`, normalized with `trim`.
examples.output: A pass — both sides are trimmed before comparison, so a real match isn't reported as a mismatch.

examples.caption: Reach a locked-down database
examples.input: A SQL query that must run from a separate secured host, sent via `DB_BRIDGE_DIR`.
examples.output: The SQL is dropped into `inbox/`, a helper on the secured host runs it and writes the result CSV to `outbox/`, and the verifier `parseCsv`s it back — no direct connection or DB driver on the running host.

underHood.heading: Takes expected and actual
underHood.whenRuns: First, for every check handed in.
underHood.input: A `ReconCheck` — name, mode, expected (source of truth), actual (under test).
underHood.output: Both sides normalized identically, if a normalize rule was given.

underHood.heading: Applies the mode
underHood.input: One of seven modes — exact, numeric-tolerance, set, contains, present, empty, count.
underHood.output: A pass/fail `ReconResult` with a plain reason — pure and offline, no DB for the comparison itself.

underHood.heading: Extracts from an API body
underHood.whenRuns: When the actual side comes from a JSON body.
underHood.input: The JSON body and a path like `data.items[*].id`.
underHood.output: The value (or list of values) at that path, ready to compare.

underHood.heading: Fetches real records
underHood.whenRuns: Only when the expected side comes from live SQL.
underHood.input: SQL text, via a direct connection or the folder-relay bridge.
underHood.output: Rows as plain objects — `parseCsv`d from the bridge's CSV when no driver is installed.

underHood.heading: Emits report evidence
underHood.whenRuns: Last, once every check has a verdict.
underHood.output: One colour-coded `EvidenceStep` per check, rendered by the shared report builder alongside API and tracker evidence.

prerequisites: Node ≥ 18 and a terminal (macOS/Linux shell or Windows PowerShell).
Node.js (installed in step 1 below) — nothing else.
No credentials, board, database, or API key are needed for the demo below — that is the point of this module. A `.env` only matters later, if you point it at something real.

steps.label: Install Node.js — the runtime.
steps.cmd:
# macOS (with Homebrew):
brew install node

# or download the LTS installer from nodejs.org, then check it worked:
node -v   # should print v18 or higher
steps.why: The toolkit is TypeScript on Node. One install per machine; no other runtime required.
steps.firstRun: First time on a new machine only.

steps.label: Clone and install dependencies.
steps.why: `npm install` pulls the toolkit's only dependency (`dotenv`) into `node_modules`. No DB driver, no cloud SDK, no auth library — which is why the demos run credential-free.
steps.firstRun: Downloads everything (seconds — the dependency list is tiny).
steps.rerun: No-op unless the dependency list changed.

steps.label: (Optional) copy the env template — only to go live later.
steps.cmd:
cp .env.example .env
# then open .env and fill in ONLY the section you need
steps.why: Skippable for the demo — every capability is off by default and the demo runs on inline sample data regardless. `.env` matters only once you point the toolkit at a real board, service, or database.

steps.label: Run the capability check.
steps.why: Prints a one-line scorecard per capability (tracker, API, database, AI) — on/off with a reason. With an empty `.env` everything reads `(off)`, which is expected: the demo needs none of them on.

steps.label: Run the DB-verification demo — reconcile a synthetic DB row against a synthetic API body.
steps.why: Feeds the real recon engine an inline synthetic 'DB row' and 'API response' and runs one check per mode — exact, numeric-tolerance, set, contains, presence, null, count — split into an all-pass group and an all-fail group, proving every mode works both ways.
steps.firstRun: Runs all 16 checks (9 passing, 7 failing on purpose) and prints a results table per group plus a summary.
steps.rerun: Fully deterministic — same inline data every time, so the same 9 pass / 7 fail. No DB, network, or state at all.

steps.label: Read the pass/fail tables.
steps.cmd:
# printed straight to the terminal — no file written:
#   EXPECTED-TO-PASS  (9/9 PASS)
#   EXPECTED-TO-FAIL  (7/7 FAIL, as intended)
#   Summary: compare modes exercised: contains, count, exact, null, numeric, presence, set (all 7)
steps.why: Each row shows the mode, the check name, and the exact detail — e.g. '|7.35-7.34| = 0.00999... <= tol 0.05' — so you see precisely why a check passed or failed, not just that it did.

inputs.name: nothing
inputs.desc: The demo defines its own synthetic `dbRow` (source of truth) and `apiBody` (value under test) inline in `examples/db/demo.ts` — no DB connection or credentials to exercise the compare engine.

inputs.name: DB_CONNECTION_STRING / DB_BRIDGE_DIR (optional, for real use)
inputs.desc: Set one in `.env` to fetch the real expected side via live SQL — direct connection or folder-relay bridge for a locked-down DB — instead of a value already in hand.

outputs.name: console tables
outputs.desc: An 'EXPECTED-TO-PASS' table (9 checks, all PASS) and an 'EXPECTED-TO-FAIL' table (7 checks, all FAIL as intended) — one row per check with its mode and plain-English detail.

outputs.name: jsonPath + parseCsv showcase
outputs.desc: Prints how `jsonPath()` extracts from a nested JSON body (e.g. `data.regions[*].name`) and how `parseCsv()` turns a bridge CSV response into rows — offline, on inline sample text.

outputs.name: summary line
outputs.desc: 'DEMO OK — recon engine ran with zero infrastructure.'

runbook.rerun: Idempotent: the compare engine is a pure function of the inline `dbRow`/`apiBody`, so reruns always print the identical 9 pass / 7 fail. Point real checks at a live `DbVerifier.scalar(sql)` result and an actual API body, and the same `compare()` / `runDbVerification()` calls reconcile your real data.
runbook.integrate: Import the pure engine directly: `import { compare, jsonPath, normalizeVal } from './src/core/db'` — `compare()` takes `{ name, mode, expected, actual }` and returns a `ReconResult` with no I/O, so it's trivially unit-testable. For a full check list, use `runDbVerification()` (`./agents/db`) with an array of `DbCheckSpec`s and an `apiBody`; each result converts to report evidence via `reconStep()`, rendering alongside API and tracker checks in the same dashboard.

video.caption: A 3-4 minute screen recording: run the DB-verification demo and watch all 7 compare modes pass and fail on cue, zero database connected.
script: Open a terminal in the qa-agent-toolkit folder.
Say: 'This is the toolkit's comparing brain — the part that checks a displayed value really matches the record behind it. No database needed for this demo.'
Run `npm run demo:db`; point at the `jsonPath` showcase lines first — pulling `data.id` and a wildcarded `data.regions[*].name` out of a JSON body.
Scroll to the EXPECTED-TO-PASS table; read out two rows: the numeric-tolerance check ('|7.35-7.34|... <= tol 0.05') and the set check (regions matching regardless of order).
Scroll to the EXPECTED-TO-FAIL table; read the same numeric check with zero tolerance now failing, and the null check catching a populated field that should have been empty.
Point at the summary line: '9/9 checks passed OK' and '0/7 checks passed, 7 failed OK (all failed as intended)'.
Point at 'compare modes exercised: ... (all 7)' — say this proves every rule in the engine actually works, both ways.
Point at the parseCsv line at the bottom; say this is the same parser the folder-relay bridge uses for a locked-down database.
Read the final line: 'DEMO OK — recon engine ran with zero infrastructure.'
Close: 'Same seven rules, pointed at a real SQL result and a real API response, are exactly what runs in production.'
